note: The standard greeting; reply وعليكم السلام.

en: and upon you peace (reply to hello)
note: Always the reply to السلام عليكم.

en: welcome to you; nice to see you

ex_en: Hi brother, where have you been?

note: Very common Libyan way of welcoming a guest; the guest often replies with the same phrase.

en: how are things? (lit. what are your conditions)
ex_ar: شن حوالك؟ إن شاء الله باهي.

en: what's new? how are you? (lit. what's your news)
ex_ar: شن أخبارك؟ من زمان ما شفتك.
ex_tr: shin akhbārik? min zamān ma shuftik.
ex_en: What's new? I haven't seen you in ages.

note: Casual, especially among young people; jaww literally = atmosphere/weather.

en: how are your affairs? how's everything?
how's your health? how are you keeping?

ex_en: How's the family? Are they well?

note: Used both as question (لاباس؟ are you OK?) and answer.

en: are you well? (lit. no harm on you)
ex_en: Are you OK? You look tired.
I'm fine thank God, and you?
note: The standard answer to كيف حالك.

ex_en: How are you? – Good, thank God.
note: bāhi is the key Libyan word for good/OK.

en: good morning (reply; lit. morning of light)
ex_en: Good morning! – Good morning to you.
Good evening, how was your day?
Good evening! – Good evening to you.

en: good night (lit. may you wake up well)
ex_en: I'm going to sleep, good night.
note: To a woman: تصبحي على خير tiSb7i; reply: وانت من أهله.

en: and you too (reply to good night)
ex_ar: تصبح على خير! – وانت من أهله.

ex_en: Bye, say hi to the family for me.
note: Very common Libyan goodbye; reply الله يسلمك.

en: God keep you safe (reply to goodbye)
note: Also used to thank someone who wished you well.

ex_en: I'm busy now, see you later.
See you at the café this afternoon.
note: From تلاقى tlāga, imperfect: نتلاقى nitlāga.

en: welcome back; glad you arrived safely
ex_ar: حمد الله على السلامة! كيف كانت السفرة؟
ex_en: Welcome back! How was the trip?
note: Said to someone returning from travel, hospital, etc. Reply: الله يسلمك.

en: where have you been? long time no see

ex_en: Long time no see! What's new?

en: where are you? where have you been?
ex_en: Where have you been? We don't see you anymore.
note: Also the usual opening on the phone.

ex_en: I missed you so much, brother!
note: Maghrebi verb توحش twa77ash 'to miss'; imperfect يتوحش yitwa77ash.

ex_en: Say hi to your mother for me.
note: Reply: يوصل yūSil (it will reach) or الله يسلمك.

en: will do (reply to 'say hi for me'; lit. it will arrive)
ex_ar: سلملي على خوك! – يوصل إن شاء الله.
ex_en: Say hi to your brother! – Will do.

en: you've brightened the place; welcome (to a guest)
note: Reply: منور بأهله mnawwar b-ahla (it's bright thanks to its owners).

en: it's bright thanks to its people (reply to نورت)
ex_en: Welcome! – Thanks, it's your company that brightens it.

ex_ar: صحيت يا خوي، والله ما قصرت.
ex_tr: Sa77ēt ya khūy, wallahi ma gaSSart.
ex_en: Thanks brother, you really did your best.
note: Very Libyan way of saying thanks (lit. 'you became healthy'). To a group: صحيتوا Sa77ētu.

en: thank you; well done (lit. may God give you health)
note: Said to someone who worked hard or did you a favour.

en: please (lit. may God keep you well)
note: More typical of Morocco/Algeria; Libyans more often say بالله or يرحم والديك.
In Libyan/Maghrebi speech العافية is also a euphemism for 'fire'; in polite phrases it means health.

en: please (lit. may God have mercy on your parents)
ex_en: Please, where is the post office?
note: Polite request, common across Libya and the Maghreb.

en: please; thank you (lit. may God keep you)
wow; how wonderful (praise, wards off envy)
note: Said when admiring someone or something to avoid the evil eye.

en: praise be to God; thank God
ex_en: I passed the exam, thank God.

en: glory be to God; how amazing
ex_en: How amazing, it's a small world.

en: in the name of God (before starting something)

ex_en: God forgive me, what kind of talk is that!

ex_ar: جدي الله يرحمه كان يحب البحر.
ex_tr: jaddi allah yir7ma kān y7ibb ilba7r.
ex_en: My late grandfather, God rest his soul, loved the sea.
note: For a woman: الله يرحمها yir7amha.
Also heard as سمحني sm7ni. Reply: مسامح msāme7 (forgiven).
Used both to apologise and to console.

en: please; here you go; come in
ex_en: Here you go, this is your coffee.
note: To a woman: تفضلي tfaDDli; plural: تفضلوا tfaDDlu.

en: go away; go on; get out
note: Literally 'outside'. Also used to urge someone on: برا امشي!

en: let's go; come on; OK then

note: Libyans use هيا as much as يلا.

ex_en: Shall I come with you? – No problem.

en: enjoy; bon appétit; wear it in good health
note: Said for food, new clothes, a haircut, a shower. Reply: الله يعطيك الصحة.
The sneezer first says الحمد لله; reply يهدينا ويهديكم الله.

ex_en: I heard you're sick, get well soon.
May God heal you and give you health.
My condolences, God rest his soul.
note: Said at funerals/mourning; reply: شكر الله سعيكم.

en: happy holidays; happy birthday (lit. every year may you be well)
ex_ar: العيد غدوة، كل عام وانت بخير.
عيدكم مبروك وكل عام وانتم بخير.
ex_en: Happy Eid and many happy returns.
Good luck in your new job.

en: it's God's will; nothing can be done
ex_en: I wanted to help you but there was nothing I could do.
note: Very common Libyan expression of resignation.

en: with pleasure; gladly (lit. on my head)
gladly; right away (lit. from my eye)
as you like; take your time
ex_ar: امشي على كيفك، ما فيش زربة.
ex_en: Go at your own pace, there's no rush.

en: as you wish; whatever you want
ex_ar: نمشوا توا ولا بعدين؟ – كيف ما تبي.
ex_tr: nimshu tawwa walla ba3dēn? – kīf ma tibbi.
ex_en: Shall we go now or later? – As you wish.
Take it easy, the road is busy.

note: Careful: in Libyan قلق galag often means 'to get bored/fed up'; context decides.

ex_en: Shame on you, leave him alone!
You missed the plane? What a pity!
Oh God, I forgot the keys!
Of course I know him, he's my neighbour.
Exactly, that's what I want to say.

en: come on, behave (lit. may God guide you)
ex_en: Come on, let your brother play.
I don't have time, figure it out yourself.
note: Imperative of دبر dabbar; imperfect يدبر ydabbir.

en: hopefully it's good news; I hope all is well
ex_ar: اتصلت بيك نص الليل؟ إن شاء الله خير!
ex_tr: ittaSlat bīk nuSS illēl? inshallah khēr!
ex_en: She called you at midnight? Hope all is well!

ex_ar: خير إن شاء الله، علاش جيت بدري؟
ex_en: Is everything OK? Why did you come early?

note: fem. كبيرة kbīra; pl. كبار kbār.
fem. صغيرة Sghīra; pl. صغار Sghār.
fem. باهية bāhya; pl. باهيين bāhyīn. The most typical Libyan word for 'good'; alone it means 'OK'.
fem. خايبة khāyba. Libyan/Maghrebi everyday word for bad.
fem. جديدة jdīda; pl. جداد jdād.

ex_en: The old city in Tripoli is lovely.
note: fem. قديمة gdīma; pl. قدام gdām. For people use كبير or شايب.
fem. سخونة skhūna. Also used for hot weather: الجو سخون.

ex_en: The house is warm in winter.

note: fem. سريعة sarī3a. 'Quickly' is often بالفيسع bilfīsa3 in Libyan.
fem. بطيئة baTī'a. Colloquially a slow person is also called ثقيل.
fem. ثقيلة thgīla; pl. ثقال thgāl.
fem. خفيفة khfīfa; خفيف الدم = funny, likeable.
fem. غنية ghaniyya; pl. أغنياء aghniyā.
fem. فقيرة fgīra; pl. فقرا fugra.
fem. مسكينة miskīna; pl. مساكين msākīn.

ex_en: Your clothes are dirty, change them.
Vegetables are cheap at the market.

note: fem. جميلة jmīla. Also used to mean 'favour': عملتلي جميل.
fem. طويلة Twīla; pl. طوال Twāl.

ex_en: The way is short from here.
note: fem. قصيرة gSīra; pl. قصار gSār.
fem. سمينة smīna; pl. سمان smān.

ex_en: I became thin after the diet.
note: fem. رقيقة rgīga. Libyan/Maghrebi for slim.
fem. ضعيفة Da3īfa; pl. ضعاف D3āf.

ex_en: These trousers are loose on me.
The volume is high, turn it down a bit.
Have the clothes dried? – Yes, they're dry.
The soup is a bit salty.

note: fem. حامضة 7āmDa. القارص is the Libyan word for lemon.

ex_en: The meat is tough, cook it more.

note: fem. خاسرة khāsra. Very Libyan; in MSA خاسر means 'loser'.

ex_en: You're wrong, it's not like that.

note: fem. مريضة marīDa; pl. مرضى marDa.

ex_en: I'm busy now, I'll call you later.
The phone is dead, it has no charge.
note: fem. ميتة mayyta; pl. موتى mōta. ميت بالجوع = starving.

ex_en: The shop is open until ten.

note: fem. عادية 3ādiyya. Very common reply meaning 'no big deal'.
fem. غريبة gharība; pl. غرب ghurb / غربا ghurba.
fem. شاطرة shāTra; pl. شطار shuTTār.
fem. غبية ghbiyya. Can be offensive.
fem. مهبولة mahbūla; pl. مهابيل mhābīl. Maghrebi; often joking.

ex_en: I'm lazy today, I don't want to work.

note: fem. نشيطة nshīTa; pl. نشاط nshāT.
fem. طيبة Tayyba. In Libyan طيب as a verb also means 'to cook'.
fem. كريمة karīma; pl. كرما kurama.
fem. بخيلة bkhīla. Also شحيح sh7ī7.

ex_en: Don't believe him, he's a liar.

note: fem. مربية mrabbya. Opposite: قليل الترباية.

ex_en: The neighbourhood is quiet at night.
This road is dangerous at night.
note: fem. خطيرة khTīra. Young people use it for 'amazing'.

ex_en: I stayed home the whole day.
The bill is a dinar short.

note: fem. جاهزة jāhza. Libyans also say واجد wājid for 'ready'.

ex_en: The sea is deep here, be careful.
That old man is our neighbour.
note: fem. شايبة shāyba; pl. شيابين shyābīn. Also noun: old man.
fem. مستعجلة mista3jla. Libyans also say عندي زربة 'I'm in a rush'.

ex_en: The plane is an hour late.
You're free, do what you want.

note: Libyan usage (in the Gulf واجد means 'a lot'). fem. واجدة wājda.

ex_en: Are you happy in your job?
I'm relaxed now after the holiday.
note: fem. مرتاحة mirtā7a. Can also mean 'well-off'.

en: in a good mood; chilled out
ex_en: I'm in a good mood today, I want to go out.
Why are you sad? What happened?
She's upset by what he said.
note: fem. مقهورة magh-hūra. Very common in Libyan for emotional hurt; ق is pronounced g here.
fem. مغبونة maghbūna. Libyan/Tunisian; noun غبنة ghubna = sorrow.

ex_en: My brother is upset with me.
My dad is angry, don't talk to him now.
note: fem. متغششة mitghashsha. Very Libyan; verb تغشش tghashshash, imperfect يتغشش yitghashshash.

ex_en: Why are you so worked up?

note: fem. تعبانة ta3bāna. Can also mean 'unwell'.

ex_en: I'm sleepy, I didn't sleep last night.
I'm bored at home, I want to go out.
note: fem. قلقانة galgāna. False friend: in Libyan it mainly means bored, not 'worried' as in MSA قلقان.

ex_en: The little one is scared of the dog.
I woke up startled by the noise.
note: fem. مخلوعة makhlū3a. Maghrebi/Libyan; verb تخلع tkhalla3 'to get a fright'.
fem. مشغولة البال. Also بالي مشغول bāli mashghūl 'I'm worried'.

ex_en: I'm really under pressure this week.
I've loved the sea since I was little.
I miss my mother a lot.
note: fem. متوحشة mitwa77sha. From توحش 'to miss'; not related to 'wild'.

ex_ar: بعد شهر في الغربة ولّيت متوحش البلاد.
ex_tr: ba3d shahr fi ilghurba wallēt mitwa77ish ilblād.
ex_en: After a month abroad I became homesick.
note: البلاد ilblād here = the homeland/home town.

ex_en: I was embarrassed to ask him.
note: fem. محشومة ma7shūma. Libyan/Maghrebi; noun حشمة 7ashma = shame, modesty.

ex_en: My daughter is shy with people.
I'm torn, what should I buy?
I'm excited for the match tonight.
Are you satisfied with the work?
I'm grateful to you for everything.

note: Also = wedding celebration in some regions.

ex_en: There are no hard feelings between us.
He said it in a moment of anger.
note: Noun related to Libyan تغشش 'to get angry'.

ex_en: Love can't be bought with money.
I'm not in the mood to go out.

en: being away from home; life abroad
ex_en: Living away from home is hard.
